transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-08-21
Start: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 28 minutes
Attendees: Maya Thompson (Redwood), Liam Park (Redwood), Sasha Iyer (candidate)

Auto-generated Summary (may be imperfect):
Maya: quick phone screen to talk about background, interest in role, basic infra/ML experience, and next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey Sasha, can you hear me okay?
[00:03] Sasha: Yep, I can hear you. Thanks for taking the time, Maya.
[00:06] Maya: Absolutely. I'm Maya, I'm on the talent team here at Redwood. I'm joined by Liam who is the hiring manager for the backend team, want to say hi Liam?
[00:14] Liam: Hey Sasha, hi. Nice to meet you.
[00:16] Sasha: Nice to meet you both.
[00:18] Maya: Cool. We scheduled for ~30 minutes, quick screen. We'll go over your recent experience, dig a bit into infra and ML ops familiarity, and then chat about logistics. Sound good?
[00:27] Sasha: Sounds good.
[00:28] Liam: Yep. Maybe start with your most recent role?
[00:31] Sasha: Sure. I'm currently at HealthSync, been there about three years as Senior Backend Engineer. My focus has been on building inference pipelines for clinical NLP models, so I've worked on model serving, caching, batching layers, AWS infra - ecs and EKS, some on-prem setups, and integrating KMS for encryption.
[00:51] Maya: Nice, that's super relevant. What frameworks are you using for model serving?
[00:55] Sasha: Mostly TorchServe early on, then we moved to a custom PyTorch + FastAPI stack with uvicorn workers. Recently I worked on optimizing kv cache behavior for chat-style models - so managing the kv cache across sharded GPUs and dealing with latency spikes.
[01:13] Liam: When you say sharded GPUs, are you talking model parallel sharding or data parallel?
[01:17] Sasha: We did a mix - tensor parallel for large model shards, but a lot of our optimizations were on the serving side: reducing copy overhead, keeping kv cache warm, reusing batch buffers. We also did quantization experiments, 8-bit qint8 using bitsandbytes in a few services.
[01:37] Liam: Cool, any experience with compilation or kernel selection stuff? like writing custom kernels or tuning low-level ops?
[01:43] Sasha: Not writing kernels personally, but I collaborated with the infra team to tune CUDA launch parameters and select cuBLAS/cutlass kernels via PyTorch flags, and we benchmarked with torch.cuda.profiler. I also worked closely with our SRE to automate kernel selection as part of CI benchmarks.
[02:03] Maya: Great. How comfortable are you with Kubernetes and private networking? We do private deployments and VPC peering for some customers.
[02:11] Sasha: Very comfortable. I ran EKS clusters, set up CNI configs, handled service accounts and IAM roles, and we did a private deployment for a hospital partner on their VPC - so I handled ingress via NLB and private subnets.
[02:27] Liam: Any exposure to cost/perf tradeoffs, like configuring batching versus latency SLOs?
[02:31] Sasha: Yeah. For real-time endpoints we used small batch sizes with async processing. For bulk inference we had larger batchers and caching. One thing I worked on was adaptive batching thresholds depending on realtime tail latency - basically if latency session exceeded X ms we tightened batch windows.
[02:50] Maya: Nice, sounds like you've seen similar problems. Quick culture/bandfit: why Redwood?
[02:54] Sasha: I like the focus on production inference and the idea of shipping reliable infra - that's exactly the type of problems I like to solve. Also the team notes and blog posts about model serving caught my eye.
[03:05] Liam: Cool. A few quick logistics: what are your comp expectations and timeline?
[03:09] Sasha: I'm looking for something in the 160-185k base range with equity; I'm available to start mid-October, but can be flexible if needed.
[03:18] Maya: That's within range for the role. Anything that would prevent you from joining a hybrid or remote setup in NA?
[03:24] Sasha: No, I'm remote but I'm based in Denver and can travel for onsite loops if needed.
[03:28] Maya: Great. Technical depth: do you want to walk us through a recent tricky bug or perf problem you solved?
[03:33] Sasha: Sure. We had a rare tail-latency issue where certain prefix patterns would blow up memory use in the kv cache due to a bug in our cache eviction policy; the cache would sometimes keep stale references to tensors on certain code paths, which led to CUDA OOMs after longer sessions. I traced it to a race in the async cache flush and fixed it by adding epoch-based reference checks and switching to pooling memory arenas, which reduced the OOMs by 90%.
[04:04] Liam: Nice, that's a good signal. Any experience running benchmarks and communicating results to product/SRE?
[04:10] Sasha: Yes, I owned the weekly perf dashboard that tracked p50/p95/p99 latency across models and wrote runbooks for regressions. We also set up automated evals against a small prompt set to detect quality regressions during quantization.
[04:25] Maya: Perfect. One last quick question: do you have experience with post-quantization quality checks or evals?
[04:30] Sasha: We did A/B tests where we sampled outputs for human review and also used automated metrics like perplexity and a task-level accuracy on downstream tasks; sometimes the automated signals weren't enough so we leaned on sampling.
[04:42] [A brief line drop - audio glitch, transcription may miss ~5s]
[04:47] Liam: About the loop: if we move forward, the next step would be a take-home coding challenge focused on systems design and a 2-hour technical loop with 3 interviews. Does that work?
[04:58] Sasha: Yep, that works.
[05:00] Maya: Okay. We'll send the coding challenge and some prep notes. Anything you want us to know or ask?
[05:06] Sasha: Just that I'm also talking to one startup doing similar infra work, but I'm most interested in the product fit here.
[05:12] Maya: Good to know. We'll aim to get the challenge over tomorrow. Thanks for your time, Sasha. We'll be in touch.
[05:18] Sasha: Thanks everyone, appreciate it.
[05:20] [End of recording]

Notes: transcription shows a couple small gaps around 4:42 due to a brief drop; otherwise conversational, natural filler (um, yeah), and minor mis-transcriptions of some technical terms (e.g., "kv cache" sometimes transcribed as "kay vee cache").
